text: Ten-year school reunion. The name badges are doing a lot of work. Your old desk-mate calls you by your sister's name.
Third wedding this summer. You own one suit, and it knows every dance floor in town. It still smells of cake.
Your friend hands you their newborn without warning. It weighs about as much as a bag of sugar. It's looking at you.
You bent down to tie a shoelace and something in your back said no. You're now shaped like a question mark.
You stayed up past midnight once, on Saturday, for reasons you can't recall. You've been paying for it since Thursday.
It's Sunday night and you already dread Monday. Your stomach knows the alarm by heart. It's been six years.
A colleague tells you what they earn, mid-sandwich. It's more than you, for the same job. They're still chewing.
An old classmate messages after eight years. There's a business opportunity, emojis, and you could be your own boss.
The landlord is raising the rent and calls it "exciting news". The boiler still bangs. The bathroom mould has a face.
Your neighbour has taken up the drums. It's going badly and it's going nightly. Tonight: one song, eleven times.
Your friend just got a new car on finance. It smells of plastic and ambition. The payments are "basically nothing".
A parent had a fall in the garden. They say it's nothing and you shouldn't fuss. They say it twice. That's the tell.
The doctor reads your numbers off a screen, doesn't look up, and says they're "fine for now". You hate the "for now".
You and your closest friend now only talk about how you never talk. The last real chat was a voice note. Mostly wind.
A glass of wine every night has quietly become two. The glasses have also got bigger. Nobody bought bigger glasses.
A friend mentions their therapist the way other people mention a good mechanic. "Honestly, life-changing. Thursdays."
A colleague's training for a marathon and needs a partner. You own trainers. Mostly you've worn them to stand in queues.
A pottery class on Tuesdays, in a cold hall that smells of wet clay. You'd finally have a hobby. Maybe even a bowl.
You've been saying "one day" about that trip for ten years. Your guidebook lists prices that no longer exist.
You find a wallet on the train: three hundred in cash and a photo of a very old dog in a very small hat.
Your workplace wants everyone as vegetables for charity. There's a sign-up sheet. Someone already took the carrot.
You find your first grey hair. It's thicker than the others, wiry, and clearly in charge. The rest will follow its lead.
A teenager on the bus calls you "sir" or "ma'am" and offers a seat. You look behind you. Nobody there. They mean you.
A friend wants you to co-sign a loan for their food truck. It's a very good truck. There's a winking taco on the side.
You ask an online calculator when you can retire. It thinks for a long while, then says 94. It adds a sad face.
You look up someone from your past at 2am. Your thumb slips and likes a photo from 2011. The little heart glows red.
You've been called for jury duty. Three weeks in a beige room with eleven strangers, a broken fan and a biscuit rota.
A friend is moving abroad and asks you to take their rat, Margaret, "just for now". Margaret has luggage. And opinions.
You sat in the car outside work for forty minutes, engine off, same advert playing. You couldn't make yourself go in.
You could pay someone to clean the gutters, or trust your grandad's old ladder. One rung is held on with tape and hope.
You turn 40. A card says you're "not old, just vintage", above a wine bottle with legs. You keep it, and you hate it.
There's a red convertible in the showroom window, leather seats warm in the sun. It knows your name. It knows your year.
The menu has got smaller. All menus have got smaller. You hold this one at arm's length while the waiter waits.
Your knee now predicts the weather, more accurately than the forecast. It clicks on the stairs. It says rain Thursday.
A letter invites you for a routine screening. It's printed in a very calm font. It uses the word "just" four times.
The nurse pumps the cuff twice, frowns at the dial, and asks about your week. You say "fine". The dial disagrees.
Your chest feels tight on the stairs. Your left arm is heavy, like it's carrying shopping. Probably nothing.
A parent has started repeating the same story, the one about the goat at the wedding. That's three times this visit.
A parent can't manage alone any more. The kettle was left on twice this week. The care home brochure smiles a lot.
The funeral's on Friday. The sandwiches are ordered. Somebody needs to say a few words, and everybody looks at you.
A friend from your twenties died. You find out from a post, wedged between a sock advert and a skateboarding dog.
The promotion went to someone born the year you started working. They have great hair and call everyone "legend".
HR invites you to a meeting about "exciting changes". You walk in. There's a box of tissues on the table.
Work has a new system. The twenty-three-year-old explaining it speaks gently, the way you'd talk to a nervous horse.
Your pension statement has arrived. The graph is not a nice shape. It's a ski slope, and you're at the bottom.
A man on the radio says it isn't too late to get rich. He sounds very tanned. His seminar costs two thousand.
A doctor says you need more exercise. The local pool has a slow lane, chlorine fumes and three very fast pensioners.
You've got your weekends back. There's a Saturday choir, or a shed at the end of the garden with a good chair.
Your school bully sends a friend request. They've found peace, a beard and a podcast, and want to talk about all three.
A local college wants mentors in your line of work. One hour a week, free coffee, and students who think you're ancient.
You've gone up a size. The jeans are winning. The shop assistant smiles kindly and calls the next size "relaxed fit".
Your hairline has moved out without telling you. No forwarding address. The wind now reaches new parts of your head.
A clinic promises to take ten years off your face. The photos look great. Your face would have to stay very still.
You could retrain and do what you wanted to do at twenty. You kept the notebook of plans. Everyone says you're mad.
A distant aunt you met twice has left you some money. And a lot of spoons. Four hundred and twelve of them.
You're invited to a party that starts at nine. At night. You're usually asleep by then, with a hot water bottle.
The doctor asks how much you drink. You halve it. The doctor, who has heard this before, doubles it and writes it down.
You're awake at 4am again, staring at the ceiling, replaying something you said in 1998. Nobody else remembers it.
Someone young is crying at the bus stop, and pretending not to. They're staring very hard at the timetable.
You've started counting the years to retirement. You have an app for it, with a progress bar. It moves very slowly.
You turn 60. Someone gives you a card with a cartoon tortoise in a party hat on it. It's a compliment, apparently.
HR sends a leaflet called 'Your Next Chapter', with a couple laughing at a salad. The chapter has a lot of white space.
The leaving do is in the pub. Thirty years of colleagues say 'we must keep in touch'. The card is signed by strangers.
It's Tuesday. No work, no plans, nobody who needs you. The kitchen clock ticks louder than it used to. The day is long.
Your child hands you a small, furious bundle. It is your grandchild. It is red in the face. It has your nose.
The grandchildren are coming for the weekend. There's one biscuit tin, one fragile vase and eight hours of energy each.
The surgeon says your hip is 'a bit worn' and shows you an X-ray like a cracked teacup. Also, you've been walking funny.
The world has gone soft and blurry. The optician says it looks like it's behind a bath curtain because it is. Fixable.
You now take eleven tablets a day. They live in a plastic box with the days of the week on it. Wednesday rattles most.
The rug moved. You went with it. You're on the floor, staring at the underside of your sofa. A biscuit lives there.
The stairs have started to look like a mountain, the bedroom at the summit. There's a bungalow on the next street.
Another name has been crossed out of the address book. You're the last who knows the funny story about the caravan.
Your partner is poorly, and the doctor says 'long term'. New pill boxes line the counter. You're now the carer.
The house is quiet in the evenings. Their chair still has the dent in it. You keep making tea for two.
You've met someone at the choir. They sing slightly flat. They laugh at your jokes. They have, frankly, excellent knees.
A polite young man from "your bank" wants your PIN, urgently. Behind him, forty other voices are asking for PINs.
Your grandchild wants to show you a thing called a 'video call'. Your face fills the screen, mostly nostril.
The allotment committee has a plot going. Fallow, they say, for 'a while'. It's a small forest. Something lives there.
The brochure says: 'Unpack once.' You like the sound of that. The tennis-court-sized buffet, even more.
The solicitor has papers and a very good pen. Who gets the house, the spoons, the cat? The cat has not been consulted.
You went upstairs for something. You are now upstairs, holding a sock. This has happened before. Twice this week.
Your grandchild holds up a phone to record you and says: 'Tell me what it was like.' It was, you realise, quite a lot.
The community hall does a tea dance on Thursdays. Two men and a keyboard play. A woman in a sequined cardigan beckons.
Your child gently shows you a brochure. A conservatory, a bingo night, and many cheerful nurses holding teapots.
You are 80. The mayor sends a card. So does the king. So does a double-glazing company, with a discount voucher.
You are 100. A reporter asks for the secret. You're tempted to say 'luck', but it's a slow news day and there's cake.
The flu is going round the street, house by house. You're being very good at getting it. The tissues are running out.
You find a box of photographs in the loft. A young person grins in every one, with terrible hair. You know that grin.
The park bench is free, and still warm from the sun. The ducks have formed a line. They look expectant.
The neighbour wants to chat over the fence. It's been twenty minutes. You now know everything about the bins.
The crossword has one clue left. Seven letters, ends in E. It's been one clue left since breakfast. The tea is cold.
Another appointment. The waiting room smells of hand gel. The magazines are from a different decade, quizzes filled in.
The phone rings. It's family, and they sound pleased you picked up. There's a lot of noise behind them, and a baby.
It's cold out and the windows have fogged. There are carrots, an onion and some beef in the fridge. A stew is possible.
The afternoon sun lies across the armchair like a warm blanket. The cushion has a dent your exact shape. It's calling.
A robin sits on the fence and watches you dig, tilting its head each time you turn the soil. It's expecting worms.
The news is terrible again. The man in the suit looks tired. You've heard all of this before, with different names.
An old song comes on while you're washing up. You remember exactly where you were, who with, and what you wore.
The stairs are a lot today. Fourteen steps, every one of them looking at you. You have a choice about how to do them.
The shop has a new self-service till. It talks to you in a cheerful voice, and it's wrong about the bananas. Again.
{boss} stops you mid-shift, loud enough for the whole floor. "Good work today, {job}." Everyone heard.
Something went wrong. The room has gone very quiet. {boss} is looking straight at you, and not blinking.
Your station is sticky, upside down, the labels swapped. You didn't leave it that way. {rival} is humming.
{rival} is telling {boss} about "their" idea, using your exact words. It was your idea. You wrote it on a napkin.
Closing time. The lights are half off. {rival} tears a stale muffin in two and holds out the bigger half to you.
There's a party on Saturday and everyone's going. You're rostered on. {friend} says they'll cover, no problem.
{friend} is sick and calls you, croaking. They beg you to cover their shift tonight, sneezing between the words.
In the break room, over the kettle, someone whispers that {boss} and {rival} are related. Same nose. It explains a lot.
Apparently you're "{boss}'s favourite". The whole shift thinks so. Chat stops when you walk into the break room.
{boss} leans in: there might be "a little extra" in your pay this year. They hold two fingers very close together.
Double shift, no break, feet throbbing. {boss} just called you "the new kid" again, in front of a customer.
{boss} wants a word, door closed. They don't sit down. "One more slip and you're done." The wall clock ticks.
Your first real pay is in your account. You check it three times on the bus home. It looks enormous.
Your shift ran late and you smell of the job. There's an assignment due at nine, and you haven't written a word.
{crush} keeps ending up on the same shift as you. Every rota, same days. Coincidence? They smile at the board.
{crush} borrows your name tag, draws a tiny smiley face on it, and hands it back without a word. Your ears go warm.
You and {crush} are alone in the break room. The vending machine hums. The kettle clicks off. Nobody is talking.
Shift's over. Everyone's gone. {crush} is lingering by the door, fiddling with their coat zip. This is it.
{crush} has started taking breaks with {rival}. They share crisps on the back step. You can hear the laughing.
{boss} doesn't know you and {crush} are together. {rival} does, and keeps winking at you both, very slowly.
You and {crush} were laughing at something stupid and the orders piled up. The printer is spitting tickets on the floor.
You and {crush} fought over text last night. You're rostered side by side all day. They're stacking cups very loudly.
Every time {crush} walks past, the room gets two degrees colder. Your coworkers have started eating lunch elsewhere.
{crush} says "we should talk" in the walk-in freezer, between the frozen peas. Your breath fogs. That's never good.
Your shift just ended and your feet ache. {partner} texts: "Milkshakes? I'm buying." Then three cow emojis.
{partner} is coming for dinner. Your family is being weird about it. Someone ironed the tablecloth. Nobody irons it.
Neither of you works there any more. No rota, no gossip. {partner} asks, honestly, what you even talk about now.
{partner} saw you laughing with someone new by the lockers and has questions. They ask them very calmly. That's worse.
{partner} sits you down on the bench where you first kissed. They think you've grown apart. They've clearly practised.
The fryer alarm has been beeping for nine minutes. The kitchen smells of hot oil and panic. Nobody knows how to stop it.
A school bus just pulled into the drive-through. Forty kids, forty orders, and one wants a milkshake with no milk.
A man wants a refund on a jumper. There's confetti in the pocket. He has very clearly worn it to a wedding.
You've folded the same table of shirts six times today, edges neat. Someone just unfolded the whole stack and left.
It's 10 p.m. The kids are still awake, wired on juice and bouncing on the sofa. You've lost the remote.
A kid in the deep end is flailing. Or waving. Hard to tell with the sun on the water. The whistle is in your hand.
Six hours in the high chair and you forgot the sunscreen. Your nose glows. Your shoulders are toast. An hour to go.
Number 42's dog is out again. It is enormous, it is sitting on the path, and it is watching you. Its tail is still.
Pouring rain at 6 a.m. The streets are dark and empty. The papers in your bag are already soggy. Your socks are next.
A regular asks for a heart in their latte and leans on the counter to watch. You've never done one. The milk is hot.
The dish pile is taller than you and starting to lean. {rival} wanders past and adds a crusty lasagne tray to the top.
